24          Plaintiff Stephen Albinda, (“Plaintiff”) brings this Class Action Complaint against

25 Defendant Activehours, Inc., doing business as EarnIn (“Defendant”) as an individual and on

26 behalf of all others similarly situated, and alleges, upon personal knowledge as to Plaintiff’s own

 1 actions and to counsels’ investigation, and upon information and belief as to all other matters, as

 2 follows:

 3                              PARTIES, JURISDICTION & VENUE

 4          1.      Plaintiff Stephen Albinda is a resident and citizen of Sioux Falls, Minnehaha

 5 County, South Dakota. Plaintiff Albinda is a user of the EarnIn platform.

 6          2.      Defendant, Activehours, Inc., dba EarnIn, is a foreign stock corporation with a

 7 principal place of business located at 391 San Antonia Road, 3 rd Floor, Mountain View,

 8 California 94040.

 9          3.      This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to the Class

10 Action Fairness Act (“CAFA”), 28 U.S.C.§1332, because this is a class action wherein the

11 amount in controversy exceeds the sum or value of $5,000,000.00, exclusive of interest and

12 costs, there are more than 100 members in the proposed class, and at least one member of the

13 class is a citizen of a state different from each Defendant.

14          4.      This Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendant because Defendant has

15 purposefully availed itself of the laws, rights, and benefits of the State of California; has

16 sufficient minimum contacts in this State; and Plaintiff’s claims arise out of or relate to

17 Defendant’s business in this State.

18          5.      Venue is proper under 28 U.S.C §1391(b) because Defendant maintains a

19 registered agent in this District, is subject to the Court’s personal jurisdiction, and a substantial

20 part of the events and omissions giving rise to Plaintiff’s claims occurred in and emanated from

21 this District.

22                                    FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

23          6.      Defendant is an earnings management company that offers a suite of tools

24 designed to give consumers access to their earnings and support financial wellness. As an

25 earnings management company, Defendant is significantly engaged in financial activities or

26 significantly engaged in activities incidental to such financial activities and requires customers to

27 provide their sensitive personal information in connection with the relevant transaction.

28

                                     CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT

 1          7.     Plaintiff and Class Members (later defined) are current and former users of

 2 Defendant’s various services and products. During their relationship, Plaintiff and Class

 3 Members provided Defendant with at least the following: name, address, Social Security

 4 number, date of birth, and bank account and routing numbers.

 5          8.     “The financial sector is an attractive target for cyber criminals not only for the

 6 immediate financial gain but also due to the wealth of sensitive customer information it holds.” 1

 7 In 2023, the financial sector accounted for 27% of the breaches handled by Kroll. 2 “In 2024, the

 8 Financial Services industry, led by Commercial Banks and Insurance, was the most breached

 9 industry, followed by Healthcare (the most attacked industry each year from 2018 until 2024).” 3

10          9.     Upon information and belief, Defendant was on notice that failing to take steps

11 necessary to secure the PII from the risk of improper disclosure left the data in a dangerous

12 condition.

13          10.    Plaintiff and Class Members, as customers of Defendant, relied on this

14 sophisticated business entity to keep their PII confidential, securely maintained, and to make

15 only authorized disclosures of this information.

16          11.    In, or around, April 2025, Defendant determined that an unauthorized party

17 accessed and acquired personal data from Defendant’s banking partner. Investigation determined

18 that the unauthorized party gained access to the personally identifiable information (“PII”) of

19 over 21,178 customers, including, but not limited to: Name, address, Social Security number,

20 and date of birth (hereafter, the “Data Breach”).

21          12.    On, or about, November 12, 2025, Defendant reported the Data Breach to the

22 Texas Attorney General.

23

24

 1           13.    Upon information and belief, the Data Breach was a direct result of Defendant’s

 2 failure to implement an information security program designed to: (a) to ensure the security and

 3 confidentiality of customer information; (b) to protect against anticipated threats or hazards to

 4 the security or integrity of that information; and (c) to protect against unauthorized access to that

 5 information that could result in substantial harm or inconvenience to any customer.

 6           14.     An information security program encompasses the administrative, technical, or

 7 physical safeguards used to access, collect, distribute, process, protect, store, use, transmit,

 8 dispose of, or otherwise handle customer information. Had Defendant implemented an

 9 information security program consistent with industry standards and best practices, it could have

10 prevented the Data Breach.

11           15.    As a result of the Data Breach, Plaintiff has suffered an actual injury, similar to an

12 intangible harm remedied at common law. Defendant’s failure to implement an information

13 security program resulted in the unauthorized disclosure of Plaintiff’s private information to

14 cybercriminals. The unauthorized disclosure of Plaintiff’s PII constitutes an invasion of a legally

15 protected privacy interest, that is traceable to the Defendant’s failure to adequately secure the PII

16 in its custody, and has resulted in actual, particularized, and concrete harm to the Plaintiff. The

17 injuries Plaintiff suffered, as described herein, can be redressed by a favorable decision in this

18 matter.

19           16.    Defendant’s conduct, as evidenced by the circumstances of the Data Breach, has

20 created a substantial risk of future identity theft, fraud, or other forms of exploitation.

21           17.    Upon information and belief, the data acquired in the Data Breach was leaked, or

22 will be leaked, on the dark web. The dark web uses a series of encrypted networks to hide users’

23 identities, which makes it convenient for criminals to buy and sell illegally obtained data. Many

24 criminals purchase stolen personal data off the dark web before launching social engineering-

25 based attacks. A social engineering attack is a method of using psychological manipulation to

26 deceive a victim and gain access to a computer system or to steal sensitive information such as

27 login credentials. Social engineering attacks that can be launched using names, telephone

28

 1 numbers and email addresses include phishing, smishing (SMS message), vishing (voice

 2 messaging), pretexting, and baiting attacks.

 3          18.     As a result of the Data Breach, Plaintiff and Class Members suffered injuries

 4 including, but not limited to: (i) invasion of privacy; (ii) theft of PII; (iii) lost or diminished value

 5 of PII; (iv) lost time and opportunity costs associated with attempting to mitigate the actual

 6 consequences of the Data Breach; (v) loss of benefit of the bargain; (vi) an increase in spam

 7 calls, texts, and/or emails; (vii) statutory damages; (viii) nominal damages; and (ix) the

 8 continued and increased risk their PII will be further misused, where their data remains

 9 unencrypted and available for unauthorized third parties to access on the dark web or otherwise.

10          19.     Specifically, Plaintiff Albinda has suffered injuries as a result of the Data Breach.

11 Plaintiff has spent and will continue spending time and effort investigating the data breach,

12 monitoring his accounts for evidence of misuse, and purchasing credit monitoring/identity theft

13 protection to mitigate the imminent and impending injury arising from the increased risk of fraud

14 or misuse stemming from the Data Breach. Plaintiff also sustained a diminution in the value of

15 his PII, which is a form of intangible property. The exposure of Plaintiff’s Social Security

16 number and/or banking information has caused Plaintiff to suffer from anxiety, stress, fear and

17 frustration regarding the real consequences of the Data Breach.

18          20.     Plaintiff brings this class action lawsuit individually, and on behalf of all those

19 similarly situated, to address Defendant’ inadequate data protection practices and for failing to

20 provide timely and adequate notice of the Data Breach.

21          21.     Through this Complaint, Plaintiff seeks to remedy these harms individually, and

22 on behalf of all similarly situated individuals whose PII was accessed during the Data Breach.

23 Plaintiff has a continuing interest in ensuring that personal information is kept confidential and

24 protected from disclosure, and Plaintiff should be entitled to injunctive and other equitable relief.

25                                     Data breaches are preventable.

26          22.     Upon information and belief, the Data Breach was a direct result of Defendant’s

27 failure to: (i) identify risks and potential effects of collecting, maintaining, and sharing personal

28

 1 information; (ii) adhere to its published privacy practices; (iii) implement reasonable data

 2 protection measures for the collection, use, disclosure, and storage of personal information; (iv)

 3 encrypt sensitive data such as Social Security numbers, and/or (v) ensure its third-party vendors,

 4 or business partners were required to implement reasonable data protection measures consistent

 5 with Defendant’s data protection obligations.

 6         23.     The Federal Trade Commission’s Standards for Safeguarding Customer

 7 Information (the “Safeguards Rule”) 16 CFR §314, requires covered financial institutions to

 8 develop, implement, and maintain an information security program with administrative,

 9 technical, and physical safeguards designed to protect customer information.

10         24.     The following recommendations should be followed:

11
                   a. Before you outsource any of your business functions investigate the
12                    company’s data security practices and compare their standards to yours. 4
                   b. Select service providers with the skills and experience to maintain appropriate
13                    safeguards. Include security expectations in vendor contracts, monitor the
14                    service provider’s work, and provide for periodic reassessments of their
                      suitability.
15                 c. Designate a qualified individual to implement and supervise the information
16                    security program.
                   d. Conduct an assessment to determine foreseeable risks and threats service
17                    providers present to the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer
                      information.
18
                   e. Design and implement safeguards to control the risks identified through the
19                    risk assessment.
20                 f. Regularly monitor and test the effectiveness of the service providers’
                      safeguards.
21
                   g. Provide security awareness training and schedule regular refreshers.
22                 h. Negotiate contracts with service providers that include clear obligations
23                    regarding data privacy and security.
                   i. Develop a plan to respond to security incidents involving service providers.
24

25

 1           25.    Given that Defendant is engaged in activities that are financial in nature, or

 2 incidental to such financial activities, Defendant could and should have identified the risks and

 3 potential effects of collecting, maintaining, and sharing personal information.

 4           26.    Without identifying the potential risks to the personal data in Defendant’s

 5 possession, Defendant could not identify and implement the necessary measures to detect and

 6 prevent cyberattacks.

 7           27.    Upon information and belief, the Data Breach occurred because Defendant failed

 8 to adequately implement one or more of the following measures to protect the confidentiality and

 9 integrity of customer information, resulting the exposure of Plaintiff’s and the Class Members’

10 PII:

11        Reasonable Safeguards

12
                    a. Regularly patch critical vulnerabilities in operating systems, software, and
13                     firmware on devices. Consider using a centralized patch management system.
                    b. Check expert websites (such as www.us-cert.gov) and your software vendors’
14                     websites regularly for alerts about new vulnerabilities and implement policies
15                     for installing vendor-approved patches to correct problems.
                    c. Assess the vulnerability of each connection to commonly known or
16                     reasonably foreseeable attacks. Depending on your circumstances, appropriate
17                     assessments may range from having a knowledgeable employee run off-the-
                       shelf security software to having an independent professional conduct a full-
18                     scale security audit.
                    d. Scan computers on your network to identify and profile the operating system
19
                       and open network services. If you find services that you don’t need, disable
20                     them to prevent hacks or other potential security problems.
                    e. Implement an awareness and training program. Because end users are targets,
21
                       employees and individuals should be aware of the threat of ransomware and
22                     how it is delivered.
                    f. Enable strong spam filters to prevent phishing emails from reaching the end
23
                       users and authenticate inbound email.
24                  g. Scan all incoming and outgoing emails to detect threats and filter executable
                       files from reaching end users.
25
                    h. Configure firewalls to block access to known malicious IP addresses.
26
                    i. Set anti-virus and anti-malware programs to conduct regular scans
27                     automatically.

28

 1               j. Manage the use of privileged accounts based on the principle of least
                    privilege: no users should be assigned administrative access unless absolutely
 2                  needed; and those with a need for administrator accounts should only use
                    them when necessary.
 3
                 k. Configure access controls—including file, directory, and network share
 4                  permissions— with least privilege in mind. If a user only needs to read
                    specific files, the user should not have write access to those files, directories,
 5
                    or shares.
 6               l. Disable macro scripts from office files transmitted via email. Consider using
                    Office Viewer software to open Microsoft Office files transmitted via email
 7
                    instead of full office suite applications.
 8               m. Implement Software Restriction Policies (SRP) or other controls to prevent
                    programs from executing from common ransomware locations, such as
 9                  temporary    folders  supporting     popular    Internet   browsers     or
10                  compression/decompression programs, including the AppData/LocalAppData
                    folder.
11               n. Consider disabling Remote Desktop protocol (RDP) if it is not being used.
12               o. Use application whitelisting, which only allows systems to execute programs
                    known and permitted by security policy.
13
                 p. Execute operating system environments or specific programs in a virtualized
14                  environment.

15               q. Categorize data based on organizational value and implement physical and
                    logical separation of networks and data for different organizational units.
16               r. Conduct an annual penetration test and vulnerability assessment.
17               s. Secure your backups.5
18               t. Identify the computers or servers where sensitive personal information is
                    stored.
19
                 u. Identify all connections to the computers where you store sensitive
20                  information. These may include the internet, electronic cash registers,
                    computers at your branch offices, computers used by service providers to
21                  support your network, digital copiers, and wireless devices like smartphones,
                    tablets, or inventory scanners.
22
                 v. Don’t store sensitive consumer data on any computer with an internet
23                  connection unless it’s essential for conducting your business.

24               w. Encrypt sensitive information that you send to third parties over public
                    networks (like the internet) and encrypt sensitive information that is stored on
25                  your computer network, laptops, or portable storage devices used by your

 4                  y. Restrict employees’ ability to download unauthorized software. Software

16          28.     Defendant knew and understood PII is valuable and highly sought after by

17 cybercriminals seeking to illegally monetize that data. At all relevant times, Defendant knew, or

18 reasonably should have known, of the importance of safeguarding PII and of the foreseeable

19 consequences that would occur if a data breach occurred, including the significant cost that

20 would be imposed on Plaintiff and the Class Members as a result.

21          29.     Upon information and belief, a criminal can easily link data acquired in the Data

22 Breach with information available from other sources to commit a variety of fraud related

23 crimes. An example of criminals piecing together bits and pieces of data is the development of
                    6
24 “Fullz” packages. With “Fullz” packages, cyber-criminals can combine multiple sources of PII

25 to apply for credit cards, loans, assume identities, or take over accounts.

26
     6
27     “Fullz” is term used by cybercriminals to describe “a package of all the personal and financial
     records that thieves would need to fraudulently open up new lines of credit in a person’s name.”
28

 1          30.     Given the type of targeted attack in this case, the sophistication of the criminal

 2 responsible for the Data Breach, the type of PII involved in the Data Breach, the ability of

 3 criminals to link data acquired in the Data Breach with information available from other sources,

 4 and the fact that the stolen information has been placed, or will be placed, on the dark web, it is

 5 reasonable for Plaintiff and the Class Members to assume that their PII was obtained by, or

 6 released to, criminals intending to utilize the PII for future identity theft-related crimes or

 7 exploitation attempts.

 8          31.     The substantial risk of future identity theft, fraud, or other exploitation that

 9 Plaintiff and Class Members face is sufficiently concrete, particularized, and imminent that it

10 necessitates the present expenditure of funds to mitigate the risk. Consequently, Plaintiff and

11 Class Members have spent, and will spend additional time in the future, on a variety of prudent

12 actions to understand and mitigate the effects of the Data Breach.

13          32.     For example, the Federal Trade Commission has recommended steps that data

14 breach victims take to protect themselves and their children after a data breach, including: (i)

15 contacting one of the credit bureaus to place a fraud alert (consider an extended fraud alert that

16 lasts for seven years if someone steals their identity); (ii) regularly obtaining and reviewing their

17 credit reports; (iii) removing fraudulent charges from their accounts; (iv) closing new accounts

18 opened in their name; (v) placing a credit freeze on their credit; (vi) replacing government-issued

19 identification; (vii) reporting misused Social Security numbers; (viii) contacting utilities to

20 ensure no one obtained cable, electric, water, or other similar services in their name; and (ix)

21 correcting their credit reports.7

22

 1          33.    Furthermore, Defendant’s poor data security practices deprived Plaintiff and Class

 2 Members of the benefit of their bargain. By transacting business with Plaintiff and Class

 3 Members, collecting their PII, using their PII for profit or to improve the ability to make profits,

 4 and then permitting the unauthorized disclosure of the PII, Plaintiff and Class Members were

 5 deprived of the benefit of their bargain.

 6          34.    When agreeing to pay Defendant for products or services, consumers understood

 7 and expected that they were, in part, paying for the protection of their personal data, when in

 8 fact, Defendant did not invest the funds into implementing reasonable data security practices.

 9 Accordingly, Plaintiff and Class Members received services that were of a lesser value than what

10 they reasonably expected to receive under the bargains they struck with Defendant.

11          35.    Through this Complaint, Plaintiff seeks redress individually, and on behalf of all

12 similarly situated individuals, for the damages that resulted from the Data Breach.

13                                      CLASS ALLEGATIONS

14          36.    Plaintiff brings this nationwide class action individually, and on behalf of all

15 similarly situated individuals, pursuant to Rule 23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

16          37.    The Class that Plaintiff seeks to represent is defined as follows:

17        Nationwide Class: All individuals residing in the United States whose PII was
         accessed or acquired by an unauthorized party as a result of a data breach that was
18       reported by Defendant in, or around, November 2025 (the “Class” or “Class
         Members”).
19

20       South Dakota Subclass: All individuals residing in the South Dakota whose PII was
         accessed or acquired by an unauthorized party as a result of the data breach that was
21       reported by Defendant in, or around, November 2025 (the “South Dakota Subclass”)

22          38.    Excluded from the Class are the following individuals and/or entities: Defendant
23 and Defendant’s parents, subsidiaries, affiliates, officers and directors, and any entity in which

24 Defendant has a controlling interest; all individuals who make a timely election to be excluded

25 from this proceeding using the correct protocol for opting out; and all judges assigned to hear

26 any aspect of this litigation, as well as their immediate family members.

27

28

 1         39.      Plaintiff reserves the right to amend the definitions of the Class or add a Class or

 2 Subclass if further information and discovery indicate that the definitions of the Classes should

 3 be narrowed, expanded, or otherwise modified.

 4         40.      Numerosity: The members of the Class are so numerous that joinder of all

 5 members is impracticable, if not completely impossible. However, the exact number of Class

 6 Members is unknown to Plaintiff at this time and such number is exclusively in the possession of

 7 Defendant.

 8         41.      Common questions of law and fact exist as to all members of the Class and

 9 predominate over any questions affecting solely individual members of the Class. The questions

10 of law and fact common to the Class that predominate over questions which may affect

11 individual Class Members, includes the following:

12
                 a. Whether and to what extent Defendant had a duty to protect the PII of Plaintiff
13                  and Class Members;
                 b. Whether Defendant had a duty not to disclose the PII of Plaintiff and Class
14                  Members to unauthorized third parties;
15               c. Whether Defendant failed to adequately safeguard the PII of Plaintiff and Class
                    Members;
16
                 d. Whether Defendant required third-party vendors to adequately safeguard the PII
17                  of Plaintiff and Class Members;
18               e. When Defendant actually learned of the Data Breach;
                 f. Whether Defendant adequately, promptly, and accurately informed Plaintiff and
19
                    Class Members that their PII had been compromised;
20               g. Whether Defendant violated the law by failing to promptly notify Plaintiff and
                    Class Members that their PII had been compromised;
21
                 h. Whether Defendant failed to implement and maintain reasonable security
22                  procedures and practices appropriate to the nature and scope of the information
                    compromised in the Data Breach;
23
                 i. Whether Defendant adequately addressed and fixed the practices, procedures, or
24                  vulnerabilities which permitted the Data Breach to occur;
25               j. Whether Plaintiff and Class Members are entitled to actual damages, statutory
                    damages, and/or nominal damages as a result of each Defendant’ wrongful
26                  conduct;

27               k. Whether Plaintiff and Class Members are entitled to injunctive relief to redress
                    the imminent and ongoing harm faced as a result of the Data Breach.
28

 1          42.     Typicality: Plaintiff’s claims are typical of those of the other members of the

 2 Class because Plaintiff, like every other Class Member, was exposed to virtually identical

 3 conduct and now suffers from the same violations of the law as each other member of the Class.

 4          43.     Policies Generally Applicable to the Class: This class action is also appropriate

 5 for certification because Defendant acted or refused to act on grounds generally applicable to the

 6 Classes, thereby requiring the Court’s imposition of uniform relief to ensure compatible

 7 standards of conduct toward the Class Members and making final injunctive relief appropriate

 8 with respect to the Classes as a whole. Defendant’s policies challenged herein apply to and affect

 9 Class Members uniformly and Plaintiff’s challenges of these policies hinges on each Defendant’s

10 conduct with respect to the Classes as a whole, not on facts or law applicable only to Plaintiff.

11          44.     Adequacy: Plaintiff will fairly and adequately represent and protect the interests

12 of the Class Members in that Plaintiff has no disabling conflicts of interest that would be

13 antagonistic to those of the other Class Members. Plaintiff seeks no relief that is antagonistic or

14 adverse to the Class Members and the infringement of the rights and the damages suffered are

15 typical of other Class Members. Plaintiff has retained counsel experienced in complex class

16 action and data breach litigation, and Plaintiff intends to prosecute this action vigorously.

17          45.     Superiority and Manageability: The class litigation is an appropriate method for

18 fair and efficient adjudication of the claims involved. Class action treatment is superior to all

19 other available methods for the fair and efficient adjudication of the controversy alleged herein;

20 it will permit a large number of Class Members to prosecute their common claims in a single

21 forum simultaneously, efficiently, and without the unnecessary duplication of evidence, effort,

22 and expense that hundreds of individual actions would require. Class action treatment will permit
